source.title: Probing the Safety Response Boundary of Large Language Models via Unsafe Decoding Path Generation
source.authors: Hao-Yu Wang; Bing-Zhe Wu; Ya-Tao Bian; Yong-Zhe Chang; Xue-Qian Wang; Peilin Zhao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful completions can be elicited using a different method: CVM-guided decoding and, separately, soft-prompt attacks. It reports harmful-response rates, but does not reproduce the fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements in the original sources.
record.gate_note: Results directly bearing on V4 are the harmful-response and refusal rates under JVD, rates after a fixed agreement-token opening, and soft-prompt attack rates. The study does not measure per-token KL, target-model fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, safety-localized parameters, or deepening training. Figure 2 cost values and Figure 3 loss curves are not harmful-response-rate outcomes; examples without a separately reported rate are not separate rows. Table 4 restates the agreement-opening result rather than supplying a distinct measure.
record.test_reason: It measures harmful-response and refusal rates when a decoding-time change (CVM-biased top-K token selection, JVD) is applied to safety-aligned models on unmodified harmful prompts. This is a decoding change aimed at defeating refusal (V4). It also measures rates after a fixed agreement prefill. It does not fine-tune targets, measure per-token KL, localize parameters or test deepening training.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude CVM-guided decoding exposes hidden unsafe paths near the original outputs of safety-aligned models: in the first tokens, after agreement tokens and after refusal tokens. They say CVM-generated texts make stronger soft-prompt attack targets, and note a success/readability trade-off. They call for finer safety alignment at both initial and deeper tokens.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a trained cost value model to bias token selection during decoding and trains image soft prompts from the resulting texts. It does not fine-tune the target model on the original harmful-example recipe or measure aligned/base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by target model and chat template. The paper also reports that increasing β raises toxic-response rates but can reduce readability; β is set to 2, 10, and 5 for Vicuna, LLaMA-2-chat, and Mistral, respectively.

fits_no_version.finding: CVM-guided outputs start with more than 25 different opening tokens, not only 'Sure'. Some responses that open with refusal text still continue into detailed harmful content. Both findings are shown only by examples, with no rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsafe continuations remain reachable after varied openings, including after an initial refusal (deeper-token vulnerability).

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study uses a model-based safety judge with human post-evaluation, but gives no uncertainty or detailed agreement statistics here. Several reported attack effects are incomplete or strongly dependent on model and chat template. The agreement-prefix experiment has no matched no-prefix condition, so it does not isolate the effect of the prefix itself.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure 2 cost values and Figure 3 soft-prompt loss curves were not recorded as outcomes for V4 because they are not harmful-response rates; unquantified examples were also not given separate rows.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of target models.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models; the first-token vulnerability claim rests on qualitative inspection.

No matched prefill versus no-prefill comparison under the same template and metric. No textual adversarial suffixes (e.g. GCG). No decoding changes other than CVM guidance (e.g. temperature or sampling sweeps). Soft-prompt attacks have no unattacked baseline.
No test of data or objective causes.

missing.what: Dependence on β: LLaMA-2-chat template B toxic rate rises from 22.85% to 28.10% as β goes from 10 to 12. Higher β makes outputs unreadable before they become harmful.
Table 4 states LLaMA-2-chat template A after the prefill defends 89.73% of attacks, falling to 71.65% with CVM. This number does not match Table 3's 28.35%; the metric is likely refusal-based.
Prefill-only harmful rate (10.27%) versus regular decoding (0.88%) for LLaMA-2-chat template A. This is a cross-table comparison of the prefill effect itself.

record.verdict_notes: JVD fine-tunes a separate value model, not the target, so it counts as a decoding-time attack under V4. β differs by model (2, 10, 5), and the appendix reports the best of two CVM training-data strategies. Both choices inflate the headline rates. The judge is LLaMA-Guard-2 plus human post-check; no uncertainty is reported. Soft-prompt and transfer rows were moved to 'none' because they compare the authors' attack with another attack and give no unattacked rate.

versions.untested_parts: No target model is fine-tuned on a few to a few hundred harmful examples.
No target model is fine-tuned on ordinary or carefully selected benign data.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.

Tests CVM-guided decoding and soft-prompt attacks, and reports rates after a fixed agreement-token prefix. It does not compare that prefix against an otherwise identical no-prefix condition, test textual adversarial suffixes, or test decoding changes other than CVM guidance.
No weight or rank localization of safety behavior is tested.
The paper discusses early-token vulnerabilities but does not test whether safety-training data or objectives cause shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety, nor its durability, is tested.

relationships.condition: Vicuna-13B under all three chat templates; Mistral-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-2-chat refusal rates under templates B/C
relationships.reason: JVD drives Vicuna to about 97-99% concrete harmful responses with 0-3% refusals. Refusals fall sharply for Mistral and for LLaMA-2-chat B/C, e.g. 84.22% to 21.72% (r1,r2,r7,r8,r13,r14,r6,r10,r12,r16,r18).
relationships.display_finding: JVD drove Vicuna to about 97–99% concrete harmful responses with 0–3% refusals, and sharply cut refusals for Mistral and for LLaMA-2-chat under templates B/C, e.g. from 84.22% to 21.72%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Vicuna-13B under all three chat templates; Mistral-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-2-chat refusal rates under templates B/C
source_check.reason: Split this mixed group: Vicuna across templates and Mistral refusal under B/C support V4; LLaMA-2 refusal remains 21.72%/22.16% under B/C, requiring limits_scope. The cited r6 is Mistral template A and leaves 36.52% refusal.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-2-chat 7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct concrete harmful-response rates; template dependence; CVM after an agreement prefill
relationships.reason: Harmful rates rise but stay incomplete: LLaMA-2 reaches 28-39% and Mistral 30-68%. Effects vary strongly by chat template. CVM after a prefill adds little or nothing (r5,r9,r11,r15,r17,r19,r20,r4).
relationships.display_finding: Harmful rates rose but stayed partial, reaching 28–39% on LLaMA-2 and 30–68% on Mistral. Effects varied strongly by chat template, and CVM after an agreement prefill added little or nothing.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: LLaMA-2-chat 7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct concrete harmful-response rates; template dependence; CVM after an agreement prefill
source_check.reason: Incomplete harmful compliance and template dependence justify the label. Correct the rationale: after the prefill, CVM raises LLaMA-2 from 10.27% to 28.35%, a substantial 18.08-point increase; Vicuna increases only from 69.80% to 70.68%.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-2-chat 7B with its standard-like chat template A
relationships.reason: JVD leaves concrete harmful responses essentially unchanged, 0.88% to 1.06% (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Concrete harmful responses barely change, from 0.88% to 1.06%.

source_check.condition: LLaMA-2-chat 7B with its standard-like chat template A
source_check.reason: The 0.88% to 1.06% increase is a small positive move, which the state rules classify as partial. The study provides no negligible-effect or non-significance finding establishing absence. Template A is the specified Human/Assistant format; its status as the model's standard template is not established.
